authorities.name: Crimes Act 1961, s.48
authorities.date_note: Enactment year; s.48 in its current form was substituted by the Crimes Amendment Act 1980. legislation.govt.nz's own indexed page title (surfaced via WebSearch) shows the current version is 'as at 27 November 2025'. Not independently re-fetched at the raw-page level this session due to a persistent bot-challenge - see verification_note.
authorities.proposition: Every one is justified in using, in the defence of himself or herself or another, such force as, in the circumstances as he or she believes them to be, it is reasonable to use. This sets a two-part test: the circumstances are assessed subjectively (as the defendant believed them to be), but the force used must be objectively reasonable given those believed circumstances - it is not enough that the defendant believed their own reaction was reasonable.

authorities.name: Murray v R
authorities.judge_or_panel: Elias CJ, William Young J, Glazebrook J
authorities.proposition: Confirms that where a jury rejects a s.48 defence solely because the force used was excessive or disproportionate - not because the defendant lacked a genuine belief that defensive force was needed at all - New Zealand law does not treat this as a partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter. The legislative scheme in ss.20, 48 and 62 provides a comprehensive framework for excessive use of force in defence, and introducing a common-law partial defence would be inconsistent with that codified scheme; if excessive self-defence is to be recognised as a partial defence, that is a matter for Parliament, not judicial development. The Court noted this position is consistent with the High Court of Australia (Zecevic v DPP (Vic)), the Privy Council (Palmer v The Queen), the House of Lords (R v Clegg), and the Supreme Court of Canada (R v Faid). Application for leave to appeal dismissed.

This session's own independent re-fetch of the same PDF also failed to decode (WebFetch's built-in extraction, not the researching agent's local pypdf method). The case's core holding was independently corroborated via WebSearch against genuine secondary sources (an Auckland University of Technology case note and a New Zealand Criminal Law Review case note), consistent with the researching agent's account.

edges.verified_via: Murray v R [2018] NZSC 15, paras 6-8, per the researching agent's pypdf extraction and independently corroborated via WebSearch this session: confirms s.48's comprehensive statutory scheme (with ss.20 and 62) leaves no room for a common-law partial defence of excessive force, distinguishing the case where no defensive belief existed at all from the case where the force used merely exceeded what was reasonable.

what_this_is_not: Two nodes covering the self-defence justification test and the closed door on excessive-force as a partial defence - New Zealand's first-ever populated Authority Graph entry in this repository. Does not cover the murder mens rea provisions (ss.167-168), the separate excess-force framework in s.62, or any other New Zealand Criminal Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
